routes.description: Establish that early Christian sources report a transformed but physically continuous risen Jesus and that their cumulative historical provenance supports occurrence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony is historically usable, bodily in meaning, and better explained by Jesus having physically risen than by the proposed alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically grounded early testimony about Jesus after death to the conclusion that the body that died was raised in transformed physical continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and other early Christian testimony preserves resurrection claims sufficiently early and coherently to bear historical weight.
Show that spiritual and glorious body language denotes transformed embodiment rather than an immaterial survival or apparition.
Connect reported appearances and geographically dispersed early teaching to identifiable witnesses or apostolic transmission.
Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan analogues and account for costly early proclamation without dissolving it into ordinary legend.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use costly adherence and continued proclamation to support the sincerity and claimed eyewitness grounding of the resurrection belief.
Treat convergence among distinct early sources and communities as support for a common antecedent resurrection tradition.

routes.description: Withhold the bodily-resurrection conclusion by applying ordinary historical analogy and challenging the meaning, provenance, and independence of the Christian testimony.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources do not historically distinguish a bodily resurrection from spiritual interpretation, legendary transmission, inherited ideology, or comparable religious narratives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant inferring an actual bodily return from death under provisional, analogy-based historical inquiry.

centralBridges.description: Apply comparison with ordinary experience and ancient religious narratives when judging the probability of an extraordinary resurrection report.
Show that Pauline flesh, spirit, and spiritual-body language does not require physical continuity with Jesus's dead body.
Challenge the authorship, consistency, independence, and apostolic pedigree of the documents and transmission chains offered as evidence.
Provide nonmiraculous explanations for uniform belief, costly commitment, martyrdom traditions, and the movement's expansion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between divine ability to resurrect and historical evidence that a resurrection actually occurred.
Identify pre-Christian or ancient structural parallels that weaken an inference from narrative uniqueness to historical occurrence.

sections.title: Historical method and extraordinary-event inference
sections.rationale: The motion requires an inference from ancient reports to an extraordinary event, making the governing historical standard and the evidential role of early reports foundational to both routes.

sections.title: Meaning of bodily and spiritual resurrection language
sections.rationale: Whether the earliest resurrection language describes transformed physical continuity or an immaterial spiritual condition bears directly on the bodily qualification in the motion.

sections.title: Provenance and coherence of Pauline testimony
sections.rationale: Pauline material is among the earliest evidence invoked, so whether its received and revealed formulations are coherent materially affects the historical foundation of the resurrection claim.

sections.title: Chronology and relevance of pagan resurrection analogues
sections.rationale: The presence or absence of earlier comparable dying-and-rising traditions affects whether the Christian accounts are treated as historically distinctive testimony or as familiar religious narrative forms.

sections.title: Independence and reliability of apostolic transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of later Christian agreement depends on whether it preserves independently grounded apostolic information or merely repeats contested attributions and normative inherited teaching.

sections.title: Martyrdom, costly commitment, and movement growth
sections.rationale: Claims about suffering and expansion can support the sincerity or origins of resurrection belief only if their historical basis and explanatory connection to the event are established.

moves.proposition: Apostolic pedigree does not establish reliable transmission because rival teachers made analogous succession claims and falsely attributed writings were widespread.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Price's response, and the resulting first-person skeptical discussion contrasts rival pedigree claims with William's preceding cumulative case.

components.text: Whether claimed apostolic lineage explains dispersed agreement and establishes reliable transmission.
Whether named teacher-disciple pedigrees authenticate an unbroken apostolic chain.

response.rationale: The move identifies the diagnostic problem that rival groups made analogous pedigree claims, so pedigree alone cannot discriminate reliable transmission.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly identifies the nondiscriminating premise and states the resulting loss of evidential force.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to pedigree's inability by itself to determine which rival succession story is true.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly acknowledges uncertainty about the rival claims and uses them only to defeat pedigree as a sufficient warrant.

charity.alternative: A succession claim may be reliable when supported by earlier, multiple, or otherwise superior evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro case must supply those discriminating features rather than relying on the formal existence of a lineage claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nondiscrimination inference is explicit: analogous rival pedigrees prevent pedigree form alone from establishing reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific rival succession examples support the challenge, though their prevalence and exact documentary basis are only summarized.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central source-criticism bridge by defeating uncorroborated succession pedigree as authentication.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately limits its conclusion and leaves open that independently supported pedigrees could still carry historical weight.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt gives rival disciple and succession claims and explicitly concludes that analogous claims cannot determine which, if any, is true.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Apostolic identities, activities, and martyrdoms are too poorly documented and dependent on late legendary narratives to support an inference to resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's question is explicitly addressed to Price, and William is then named before giving the following rebuttal to this skeptical answer.

components.text: Whether identifiable apostles and later traditions provide a sufficiently documented chain for claims about activity and martyrdom.
Whether later geographically dispersed traditions reliably preserve knowledge about particular apostles.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the identity and documentation of the apostles and attributes much later biographical material to legendary acts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the historical-documentation demand, though it treats diverse apostolic traditions somewhat collectively.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical claim is clear, but statements that nothing is known about the apostles are broader than the cited late acts establish.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The late legendary acts justify substantial caution, while near-total agnosticism about every apostle is somewhat stronger than shown.

charity.alternative: Sparse and legendary later biographies can still preserve some earlier reliable memories about apostolic identity or death.
charity.decisiveQualification: Individual claims require earlier corroboration before martyrdom traditions can support the resurrection inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Late legend-laden sources rationally weaken martyrdom inferences, with overbroad claims about all apostolic knowledge as the main gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several second- and third-century acts are specifically identified, but the dating and evidence for each martyrdom are not differentiated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally supports source criticism by attacking the documentation behind apostolic identity, activity, and death.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows historical uncertainty rather than declaring every tradition false, though its sweeping phrasing understates possible residual knowledge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites varying apostolic lists and late Acts of Paul, Thomas, Peter, and John as fanciful sources of later claims.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Martyrdom demonstrates sincerity rather than truth, while social service, demographic practices, accessibility, and ordinary conversion dynamics can explain Christianity's growth.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Price, the answer develops his characteristic analogical skepticism, and the moderator then explicitly turns to William.

components.text: Whether widespread agreement and expansion are best explained by apostolic transmission of bodily-resurrection testimony.
Whether costly adherence to inherited teaching establishes the truth of its historical content.

response.rationale: The move answers costly commitment and growth with sincerity and social mechanisms, but does not directly test the geographic transmission links themselves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it supplies strong contrary explanatory material while leaving the selected convergence premise mostly untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between sincerity and truth is explicit, and the growth explanation is presented as a plural set of contributing mechanisms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers ordinary growth mechanisms as plausible contributors rather than claiming to prove one exclusive natural history.

charity.alternative: Martyrdom and growth may corroborate sincere testimony connected to unusually early eyewitness claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity and expansion cannot establish the testimony's truth unless the eyewitness connection and alternative growth mechanisms are separately assessed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between sincere belief and truth is explicit, and the proposed social mechanisms coherently undercut exclusivity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete social and demographic mechanisms are identified, though their comparative historical magnitude is not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central natural-explanations bridge for martyrdom, commitment, conversion, and movement growth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the sincerity inference and targets only the further transition from commitment or expansion to historical truth.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes willingness to die from truth and identifies social appeal and conversion dynamics as ordinary growth mechanisms.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Costly conversions and sustained proclamation under persecution are best explained by contact with eyewitness testimony that Jesus was physically alive after death.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to William, who answers Price by discussing Paul, Ignatius, eyewitness contacts, Justin Martyr, and persecution in one continuous turn.

components.text: Whether sincerity, social benefits, and ordinary conversion mechanisms adequately explain costly early proclamation and expansion.
Whether the relevant persecuted converts and proclaimers are historically documented and connected to eyewitnesses.
Whether claimed eyewitness contact discriminates reliable transmission from rival pedigree claims.

response.rationale: The move contacts the natural-explanation challenge by adducing persecution and claimed eyewitness access, but does not compare those factors with Price's specific growth mechanisms.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive costly-proclamation component while leaving the broader natural-growth explanation substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The costly eyewitness explanation is clear, but massive persecution, eyewitnesses, and best explained are broader than the excerpt documents.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Cost and claimed access can support sincerity, but the leap to physical resurrection as the best explanation lacks comparative exclusion of alternatives.

charity.alternative: Sincere persecuted converts may rely on inherited testimony, visions, or community belief without personally verifying a bodily resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro inference requires documented direct witness contact and evidence that those contacts reported tangible physical continuity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cost plus eyewitness contact can support sincerity and provenance, but does not without further premises establish bodily resurrection as best explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul, Ignatius, Justin, and persecution are named, while direct contacts, chronology, and the physical content of testimony remain asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the natural-explanations bridge by proposing eyewitness-grounded costly proclamation as the superior explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invokes eyewitnesses but materially compresses the strongest distinction between contact with believers and verification of the event.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes claimed eyewitnesses, Justin's costly conversion during persecution, and continued efforts to proclaim resurrection evidence.
